title: Stream joins and complex event processing
goal: By the end you can say what state each kind of stream join keeps and for how long, explain why joining a stream with the latest row of a table gives answers that depend on arrival order and fix it with a versioned table or a temporal join, read a table-table join as a materialized view that maintains itself, catch a co-partitioning mistake that Kafka can't, and describe complex event processing as a stored query with the data flowing past.

warmup.q: An order placed at 09:30 reaches a Kafka Streams join with an ordinary `KTable` of customer tiers at 10:01. The customer was upgraded from silver to gold at 10:00, and that record arrived at 10:00. Which tier does the order get?
options: Silver: Kafka Streams joins by the order's timestamp
Gold: the table holds one row per customer, the latest to arrive
None: the order is dropped as late
It depends on the grace period of the table
warmup.why: An unversioned `KTable` keeps only the latest row per key, by arrival, so the 09:30 order is joined with gold. A grace period exists for this join only with a versioned table, and it is set on the order side. A versioned table would answer silver, the version in force at 09:30. Section 2 shows why the unversioned answer also changes from one run to the next.

sections.h: Every stream join keeps one side in state and probes it with the other
sections.body:
A card authorization arrives on the `authorizations` topic at 10:00. Its capture, the merchant's request to actually move the money, arrives on `captures` at 10:04. Settlement wants one line per payment: captured, or never captured. In a database you'd write `authorizations LEFT JOIN captures USING (payment_id)` and run it once over two finished tables. A stream never finishes. When an authorization arrives, its capture may come in four minutes, in three days, or never. It may even come first, if the captures topic happens to be ahead.

The simplest join that could work keeps every record it has ever seen from both sides, indexed by key. Each new record looks up the other side's index, emits a result for every match, and adds itself to its own index. That's a hash join that never stops building its hash table. It gives the right answer, and its state grows without end: at 3,000 authorizations a second, a year of both topics is about 190 billion records.

So you decide how long a record may still find its partner. That's a window, the idea from lesson 4 of this track: a stream-stream join pairs only records whose timestamps are close enough, and throws away state that has fallen out of the window, measured in stream time. In Kafka Streams the window is a `JoinWindows`:

```kotlin
authorizations.leftJoin(
    captures,
    ValueJoiner { auth, capture -> if (capture == null) "$auth NOT CAPTURED" else "$auth captured $capture" },
    JoinWindows.ofTimeDifferenceAndGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(10), Duration.ofMinutes(1)),  // either side first, 10 min apart
    StreamJoined.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()),
)
```

Each side's records sit in a window store for 10 minutes plus 1 minute of grace, then expire. A real capture window is days long, and the state grows with it. The left join also answers the question an inner join can't: which authorizations were never captured. It can only say so after the window has closed, so "not captured" comes out late by design. Copying the authorization's fields into the capture event is no substitute: it tells you about captured payments only, and the ones you most want to see have no capture event to carry them.

That gives the picture for the rest of the lesson. **Every stream join keeps state built from one input and probes it with the other**, and the kinds of join differ only in how long that state lives, as the figure shows. A stream-stream join keeps a window of each side. A stream-table join keeps the whole table, latest row per key, and nothing of the stream. A table-table join keeps both tables.

try.title: Join authorizations with captures in a window
steps: Run `WindowJoinDemo` from the `labs` folder (command below). No broker: `TopologyTestDriver` runs the join in your JVM.
Arrival 4 is a capture for p-3 that arrives before p-3's authorization. Predict: does the join still pair them?
Predict when p-2, which is never captured, comes out as `NOT CAPTURED`: at once, at 10:11, or only after some later record?

code.title: WindowJoinDemo.kt
code.src:
package sfz.stream.l06.demo

import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.Serdes
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
import org.apache.kafka.streams.StreamsBuilder
import org.apache.kafka.streams.kstream.Consumed
import org.apache.kafka.streams.kstream.JoinWindows
import org.apache.kafka.streams.kstream.Produced
import org.apache.kafka.streams.kstream.StreamJoined
import org.apache.kafka.streams.kstream.ValueJoiner
import java.time.Duration

/**
 * A stream-stream join: each card authorization with its capture, if the capture comes within 10 minutes of it
 * (either side may arrive first), with 1 minute of grace for late records. A left join, so an authorization with
 * no capture comes out too, once its window has closed.
 */
fun main() {
    val builder = StreamsBuilder()
    val captures = builder.stream("captures", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()))
    builder.stream("authorizations", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()))
        .leftJoin(
            captures,
            ValueJoiner<String, String?, String> { auth, capture -> if (capture == null) "$auth NOT CAPTURED" else "$auth captured $capture" },
            JoinWindows.ofTimeDifferenceAndGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(10), Duration.ofMinutes(1)),
            StreamJoined.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()),
        )
        .to("auth-outcomes", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()))

    drive(builder.build(), "window-join-demo") { driver ->
        val auths = driver.createInputTopic("authorizations", StringSerializer(), StringSerializer())
        val caps = driver.createInputTopic("captures", StringSerializer(), StringSerializer())
        val out = driver.createOutputTopic("auth-outcomes", StringDeserializer(), StringDeserializer())
        println("join state: " + driver.allStateStores.keys.sorted())
        val arrivals = listOf(
            Triple("auth", "p-1", "10:00"), Triple("auth", "p-2", "10:01"), Triple("capture", "p-1", "10:04"),
            Triple("capture", "p-3", "10:05"), Triple("auth", "p-3", "10:03"), Triple("auth", "p-4", "10:20"),
            Triple("capture", "p-4", "10:22"),
        )
        for ((i, a) in arrivals.withIndex()) {
            val (kind, payment, time) = a
            if (kind == "auth") auths.pipeInput(payment, "auth@$time", at(time)) else caps.pipeInput(payment, "@$time", at(time))
            val emitted = out.readKeyValuesToList().joinToString { "${it.key}: ${it.value}" }
            println("%d. %-7s %s at %s  ->  %s".format(i + 1, kind, payment, time, emitted.ifEmpty { "(nothing yet)" }))
        }
    }
}

try.expect:
```text
join state: [KSTREAM-JOINTHIS-0000000004-store, KSTREAM-OUTEROTHER-0000000005-store, KSTREAM-OUTERSHARED-0000000004-store]
1. auth    p-1 at 10:00  ->  (nothing yet)
2. auth    p-2 at 10:01  ->  (nothing yet)
3. capture p-1 at 10:04  ->  p-1: auth@10:00 captured @10:04
4. capture p-3 at 10:05  ->  (nothing yet)
5. auth    p-3 at 10:03  ->  p-3: auth@10:03 captured @10:05
6. auth    p-4 at 10:20  ->  p-2: auth@10:01 NOT CAPTURED
7. capture p-4 at 10:22  ->  p-4: auth@10:20 captured @10:22
```
(Kafka Streams also prints a warning that these stores have generated names; lesson 5's "name your stores" note says why that matters.) The join keeps three window stores: one per side, plus one for left records still waiting for a match. The window is symmetric, so p-3's early capture waited in its store and matched when the authorization came. p-2's window closed at 10:01 + 10 min + 1 min of grace = 10:12 in stream time, but nothing moved stream time past 10:12 until p-4's authorization at 10:20. Only then did the join emit `NOT CAPTURED`.

refs.title: Kafka 4.4 Streams DSL: joining, co-partitioning and versioned tables

sections.h: A stream-table join answers with the table as it is now, unless you keep its history
sections.body:
Enrichment is the join you'll write most often. Each order needs the customer's loyalty tier, because the tier sets the cashback rate. The tiers live in the customer service's database, and change data capture (lesson 1 of this track) streams every change to the `customer-tiers` topic, keyed by customer id.

Version 1 calls the customer service for every order. At 3,000 orders a second and 5 ms per call, that's 15 calls in flight at all times, and the customer database answers every one of them. Version 2 keeps a local copy: a `KTable` built from the `customer-tiers` changelog (lesson 5). Each order looks up its customer's row on local disk in microseconds. Only orders produce output. A tier update changes the row and emits nothing, so orders already joined keep the tier they got.

Now add time. Customer c-1 was silver until 10:00 and gold after. An order placed at 09:30 sits in a lagging partition and reaches the join at 10:01, after the upgrade record. The `KTable` has one row per customer, so it answers gold, and the order earns cashback the customer didn't have when buying. Worse, the answer depends on arrival order. Rebuild the output next week from the same topics and the partitions may interleave the other way, so the same order comes out silver. A join whose result depends on arrival order isn't deterministic: two runs over the same data disagree. The stepper walks through it.

The fix is to keep the table's history and join each order with the version that was in force at the order's own timestamp. Data warehouses call this a slowly changing dimension. Kafka Streams (since 3.5) calls it a **versioned table**: materialize the table in a versioned store, and a stream-table join picks the version with the latest timestamp at or before the stream record's timestamp.

```kotlin
val tiers = builder.table("customer-tiers", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()),
    Materialized.`as`(Stores.persistentVersionedKeyValueStore("tiers", Duration.ofDays(7))))  // 7 days of history
```

It has two limits. History is bounded: an order more than 7 days older than the table's newest record can't be answered, so an inner join drops it and a left join joins it with null. And versions fix late orders, not late table updates. If the upgrade record itself arrives after an order stamped 10:02, the order gets silver, the latest version known at that moment. A grace period on the stream side, `Joined.withGracePeriod(...)` on a versioned table, holds each order that long in stream time so a slightly late update can still be used. Every order then comes out later by the grace period.

Flink SQL offers the same choices by name. An event-time temporal join, `FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF o.order_time`, joins each order with the version of a versioned table valid at that time, and waits for watermarks on both sides (lesson 4), so the watermark plays the grace period's role. A processing-time temporal join uses the latest version and has the unversioned table's problem. A lookup join queries an external database for every row, which is version 1 again.

```sql
SELECT o.order_id, o.amount, t.tier
FROM orders AS o
LEFT JOIN customer_tiers FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF o.order_time AS t
  ON o.customer_id = t.customer_id;
```

sections.h: A table-table join is a materialized view that maintains itself
sections.body:
Some joins have no stream side at all. The authorization path wants one lookup: card id to the tier of the account that owns the card. Cards come from the card service (card id to account id), tiers from the customer service (account id to tier), both as changelog topics. The output is a table too, and its changelog is a topic other services can read.

The Storage track's lesson on materialized views set up exactly this problem: a stored query result that must follow its inputs. `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW` recomputes the whole join on a schedule and is stale in between. Incremental maintenance applies each change as a delta. A table-table join in a stream processor is incremental maintenance that never stops. Each side keeps its table in a state store, and a change on either side is joined with the current state of the other. The change to a join follows the product rule from calculus:

```text
change(cards ⋈ tiers) = change(cards) ⋈ tiers  +  cards ⋈ change(tiers)
```

The processor applies one change at a time, so the term where both sides change at once never comes up.

The second term is where the cost hides. One tier change for an account with 4 cards emits 4 view updates. A fee change on a merchant category that 200,000 merchants belong to emits 200,000. Deletes come out as tombstones: delete a card, and the view emits `card-2` with a null value, which a compacted topic downstream turns into a delete (the Messaging track's lesson on compaction).

Kafka Streams has two forms. A `KTable`-`KTable` join on the primary key needs both tables keyed by the same id and co-partitioned (next section). A **foreign-key join** (since Kafka 2.4) joins on a field of the left table's value. Here the extractor returns the card's account id, the key of the tiers table:

```kotlin
cards.join(tiers, Function { account -> account }, ValueJoiner { account, tier -> "$account $tier" })
```

Kafka Streams routes the changes through internal topics so that each card meets its account's tier whatever partition either is in. That costs extra topics and a round trip through Kafka for every change. Streaming databases such as Materialize and RisingWave build whole SQL views from joins like these (the Derived data track's lesson on unbundling the database comes back to them).

try.title: A view that maintains itself
steps: Run `ViewJoinDemo`. It joins a cards table with an account-tiers table on the card's account (a foreign-key join) and prints how the view changes after each input change.
Predict before you read: when acct-1 becomes gold, how many view rows change? And when acct-1's tier is deleted?

code.title: ViewJoinDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
tiers: acct-1 silver, acct-2 gold  view changes: none
cards: card-1, card-2 on acct-1    view changes: card-1 -> acct-1 silver, card-2 -> acct-1 silver
card: card-3 on acct-2             view changes: card-3 -> acct-2 gold
tier: acct-1 becomes gold          view changes: card-1 -> acct-1 gold, card-2 -> acct-1 gold
card: card-3 moves to acct-1       view changes: card-3 -> acct-1 gold
card: card-2 is deleted            view changes: card-2 -> (deleted)
tier: acct-1 is deleted            view changes: card-1 -> (deleted), card-3 -> (deleted)
```
(Warnings about generated store names trimmed.) Tiers alone change nothing: this is an inner join, and no card points at them yet. A change on the right side fans out to every card of that account: one input change, two output rows. Moving card-3 is a left-side change, joined with the current tier of its new account. Deletes on either side come out as tombstones, the value `null`.

refs.title: Kafka 4.4 Streams DSL: joining, co-partitioning and versioned tables

sections.h: Both sides of a join must land in the same partition, and Kafka checks only half of that
sections.body:
A Kafka Streams app doesn't run one join. It runs one per task, and task 0 joins partition 0 of `orders` with partition 0 of `customer-tiers` and sees nothing else (lesson 5 introduced tasks). So an order meets its customer's tier only if both records sit in the same partition number. Two things decide that: the partition count, and the partitioner, the function from key to partition. The Java producer's is murmur2 of the key bytes modulo the count (the Messaging track's lesson on keys and partitions). Inputs that agree on both are **co-partitioned**.

Change the count and joins fail without a word. With orders on 3 partitions and tiers on 2, about two keys in three land on a different partition number, so two orders in three find no tier. Kafka Streams catches this one: when the app starts and its tasks are assigned, it compares the partition counts of the topics a join reads and throws an exception instead of running.

It can't catch a different partitioner. Suppose the tiers come from a service written in Go or Python on librdkafka, whose default partitioner (`consistent_random`) hashes keys with CRC32. With 3 partitions on both sides, two keys in three still land elsewhere, every check passes, and the joins come out with null tiers. Set `partitioner=murmur2_random` in those clients, which the librdkafka docs describe as equivalent to the Java producer's default. And growing a topic breaks co-partitioning too: going from 6 to 12 partitions moves about half of its keys, so every topic you joined it with is now mismatched, and per-key order breaks for good measure.

There are three ways out.

1. Repartition one side to match: `repartition(Repartitioned.numberOfPartitions(3))` writes it through an internal topic with the right count, for one extra write and read per record.
2. For table-table joins, use a foreign-key join, which repartitions internally.
3. Make the small side a **GlobalKTable**. Every instance reads all partitions of `customer-tiers` into a full local copy before it processes anything, so any task can look up any customer, and the join can use any field of the order as the lookup key.

The global table has its price. Every instance stores and reads the whole table: fine for 2 million customers at about 50 bytes each, 100 MB, and not for 2 billion. Start-up waits for the full copy to load. And a `GlobalKTable` has no notion of time: its joins always use the row it holds now, so section 2's versioning fix isn't available. The lab has you build both and write the start-up check yourself.

try.title: Count the orders that would miss
steps: Run `CoPartitionDemo`. It places 10,000 customer keys in two topics and counts the keys that land on a different partition number in the second one.
Predict the four percentages first. Which of the four cases would Kafka Streams refuse to start with?

code.title: CoPartitionDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
c-42: partition 0 of 3 in orders, partition 0 of 2 in customer-tiers
orders 3, tiers 3, both Java producers             0 of 10000 keys on a different partition (0.0%)
orders 3, tiers 2, both Java producers          6712 of 10000 keys on a different partition (67.1%)
orders 6, tiers grown from 6 to 12              5006 of 10000 keys on a different partition (50.1%)
orders 3 (Java), tiers 3 (librdkafka default)   6688 of 10000 keys on a different partition (66.9%)
```
c-42 happens to agree, which is why a quick manual test can pass. With 3 and 2 partitions a key agrees only when its hash modulo 6 is 0 or 1, one time in three. Doubling a topic keeps a key in place only when its hash modulo 12 is below 6, half the time. Kafka Streams refuses the second and third cases at start-up because the counts differ. The fourth has equal counts and a different hash, so it starts and quietly loses two joins in three.

sections.h: Complex event processing stores the query and lets the data flow past
sections.body:
A database stores data and runs queries that come and go. **Complex event processing** (CEP) turns that around: the query is stored and long-lived, and the events flow past it. Card testing is the classic payments case. A fraudster with a list of stolen card numbers tries small purchases until one is approved, so "three declines in a row, then an approval, within 2 minutes, on one card" is worth an alert.

You could build that from three windowed self-joins of the authorization stream. It's simpler as a pattern, compiled into a small state machine per key: 0, 1, 2 or 3 declines seen. A decline moves one state up. An approval in state 3 is a match, and an approval in any other state goes back to 0. A partial match older than 2 minutes is dropped. The state per card is tiny, the timestamps of up to three declines, and nothing else about the events is kept. The Try-it runs that machine in plain Kotlin.

FlinkCEP, Flink's pattern library, says the same thing declaratively:

```java
Pattern<Auth, ?> cardTesting = Pattern.<Auth>begin("declines")
        .where(SimpleCondition.of(a -> !a.approved()))
        .times(3).consecutive()                         // three declines in a row
        .next("approval")                               // and the very next event is an approval
        .where(SimpleCondition.of(Auth::approved))
        .within(Duration.ofMinutes(2));                 // all within 2 minutes
PatternStream<Auth> matches = CEP.pattern(auths.keyBy(Auth::card), cardTesting);
```

`next` means strict contiguity: the very next event of that card. `followedBy` would allow other events in between. In event time, FlinkCEP buffers events and evaluates them in timestamp order as the watermark passes (lesson 4), and treats an event behind the watermark as late: dropped, or sent to a side output. Esper, a CEP engine for Java and .NET that has been around for years, writes patterns in an SQL-like language called EPL, and Flink SQL has `MATCH_RECOGNIZE`, the SQL standard's syntax for row patterns.

Search on streams makes the same turn for text. A media-monitoring service stores thousands of saved searches and matches every incoming article against all of them. Elasticsearch's percolator does this: you index the queries themselves, in a field of type `percolator`, then send a document and get back the stored queries it matches. For payments, the stored queries could be sanctions-screening rules, run against the name on every new payee:

```json
{ "query": { "percolate": { "field": "rule", "document": { "payee_name": "Northwind Trading LLC" } } } }
```

The percolator matches every request fresh (it caches nothing), so send documents in batches, and avoid `wildcard` queries among the stored ones: they defeat the term extraction it uses to skip queries that can't match.

steps: Run `CepDemo`. It feeds 12 authorization results for four cards through the card-testing pattern and prints each card's state after every event.
card-4 also has three declines and then an approval. Predict whether it matches, and why.

code.title: CepDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
10:00:00 card-1  declined state 1 declines
10:00:05 card-2  approved state 0 declines
10:00:20 card-1  declined state 2 declines
10:00:41 card-1  declined state 3 declines
10:00:50 card-1  approved state 0 declines MATCH card-1: 3 declines from 10:00:00, approved at 10:00:50
10:01:00 card-3  declined state 1 declines
10:01:10 card-3  declined state 2 declines
10:01:20 card-3  approved state 0 declines
10:01:40 card-4  declined state 1 declines
10:02:10 card-4  declined state 2 declines
10:02:40 card-4  declined state 3 declines
10:04:10 card-4  approved state 0 declines
```
card-1 matches: three declines and an approval in 50 seconds. card-3's approval comes after only two declines, so it resets. card-4 reaches state 3, but its approval comes 150 seconds after the first decline, more than the 2 minutes allowed, so the partial match was dropped. Each card's state never holds more than three timestamps.

refs.title: FlinkCEP 2.3: complex event processing for Flink

analogy: A travel-expenses clerk checks each claim against the per-diem rates pinned on the wall. Most claims arrive the week of the trip and get this month's rate, which is right. A claim for a March trip that turns up in June gets June's rate, which is wrong, and the result depends on how long the claim sat in someone's inbox. A careful clerk keeps a binder of every rate sheet with the date it took effect and looks up the sheet in force on the trip's date: that's the versioned table. A clerk who also waits a few days before filing claims, in case a new rate sheet is still in the post, is using a grace period. The analogy breaks at the binder: the clerk keeps every sheet forever, while a versioned store drops history older than its retention, and a claim older than that gets no rate at all.
in_your_world: Your payments services have all three joins. Authorizations against captures is a stream-stream join, and the useful output is the left join's "never captured" line, which settlement and the finance team chase. Enrichment is everywhere: the merchant's risk tier for the fraud check, the customer's tier for cashback, and the FX rate for a cross-currency payment, which must be the rate at the payment's time or your reconciliation against the card scheme drifts. That last one is the textbook temporal join. Build it on a versioned table with enough history to cover your worst consumer lag, and test it in `TopologyTestDriver` with records piped out of order, not only in timestamp order. Check co-partitioning whenever a topic you join is produced by a non-JVM service: a Go or Node producer on librdkafka hashes keys with CRC32 unless you set `partitioner=murmur2_random`, and Kafka Streams will start happily and miss two joins in three. For small reference data, such as merchant category codes, a `GlobalKTable` in your Quarkus service avoids co-partitioning altogether.
mistake: Enriching a stream with an ordinary `KTable` and testing it with records piped in timestamp order. The tests pass, because in a test every tier update arrives before the orders that follow it. In production a lagging partition, a rebalance or a replay delivers some orders after a later tier change, and they're joined with a tier they never had. Nothing fails, and a rebuild from the same topics gives different results. People do it because the unversioned table is the default and the docs' first join example uses one. The fix: materialize the table in a versioned store (`Stores.persistentVersionedKeyValueStore`) with history longer than your worst lag, add a stream-side grace period if the table's own updates can arrive late, and add a test that pipes an old order after a newer table record.

compare.title: The same as-of join in Kafka Streams and Flink SQL

a.label: Kafka Streams
a.title: versioned table plus grace
a.src:
val tiers = builder.table("customer-tiers", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()),
    Materialized.`as`(Stores.persistentVersionedKeyValueStore("tiers", Duration.ofDays(7))))

builder.stream("orders", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()))
    .leftJoin(tiers,
        ValueJoiner { order: String, tier: String? -> "$order tier=${tier ?: "none"}" },
        Joined.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String(), Serdes.String())
            .withGracePeriod(Duration.ofMinutes(5)))     // wait for late table updates
    .to("orders-enriched")

b.label: Flink SQL
b.title: event-time temporal join
b.src:
-- customer_tiers is a versioned table: a primary key and an event-time attribute
SELECT o.order_id, o.amount, t.tier
FROM orders AS o
LEFT JOIN customer_tiers FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF o.order_time AS t
  ON o.customer_id = t.customer_id;
-- results wait for the watermarks of both inputs

compare.note: Both pick the version valid at the order's timestamp, and both have to wait for late table updates. They wait on different clocks. Kafka Streams holds each order for a grace period measured in its own stream time, and keeps a bounded history (7 days here). Flink waits until the watermarks of both inputs pass the order's time, so the watermark strategy you chose in lesson 4 decides how late a tier update may be. Flink also needs the table's primary key in the join condition. Kafka Streams needs both topics co-partitioned; Flink shuffles the inputs by the join key itself.

worked.title: Convert each payment with the FX rate in force when it was made

steps.say: Name the inputs and their keys. `payments` is keyed by payment id and carries a currency and an amount; `fx-rates` is a changelog of rates keyed by currency, each record stamped with the time the rate took effect. The join key is the currency, so the payments must be re-keyed first.
steps.code:
val payments = builder.stream("payments", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), paymentSerde))
    .selectKey { _, p -> p.currency }                       // join on currency, not payment id

steps.say: Make the re-keyed stream co-partitioned with the rates. `fx-rates` has 6 partitions; `repartition` writes the payments through an internal topic with the same count, so payment and rate for EUR meet in the same task.
Keep the rates' history. Size it from the worst lag you expect between a payment's timestamp and its arrival: if a consumer can be a day behind, keep at least a day. Here 3 days.
steps.code:
val rates = builder.table("fx-rates", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Double()),
    Materialized.`as`(Stores.persistentVersionedKeyValueStore("fx-rates", Duration.ofDays(3))))

steps.say: Join with a grace period, because rate updates can also arrive late (the rates feed batches them every few seconds). Each payment waits 30 seconds of stream time, then uses the rate in force at its timestamp.
steps.code:
byCurrency.join(rates,
    ValueJoiner { p: Payment, rate: Double -> p.copy(amountEur = p.amount * rate) },
    Joined.with(Serdes.String(), paymentSerde, Serdes.Double()).withGracePeriod(Duration.ofSeconds(30)))
    .to("payments-eur", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), paymentSerde))

steps.say: Test the late case, not only the happy path. Pipe both rates, then a payment stamped between them that arrives after both, then a later payment to move stream time past the grace period. The first payment must use the old rate. Write a second test where the 10:00 rate arrives after a 10:02 payment, and assert the grace period let that payment use it.
steps.code:
rateIn.pipeInput("USD", 0.92, at("09:00"))
rateIn.pipeInput("USD", 0.95, at("10:00"))
paymentIn.pipeInput("p-1", payment(100.0, "USD"), at("09:30"))   // a late payment: must use 0.92
paymentIn.pipeInput("p-2", payment(100.0, "USD"), at("10:05"))   // moves stream time past 09:30 + 30 s
assertThat(out.readValue().amountEur).isCloseTo(92.0, within(0.001))

lab.title: Fix a time-dependent join and check co-partitioning
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. Ten of the eleven fail. No broker: `TopologyTestDriver` runs your topologies in the test JVM.

`TierEnrichment.build()` is the buggy join from section 2: orders left-joined with an unversioned table of tiers. Read the failing test `an order that arrives after the upgrade...` and see it get gold. Fix the table: materialize it in a versioned store named `STORE` with `HISTORY` of history. The arrival-order test then runs the same records in 12 random orders and expects one answer.
Write `buildGlobal()`: the same enrichment against a `GlobalKTable`, looked up by the order's key.

In `CoPartitioning.kt`, write `partitionFor` (the Java producer's formula; a test compares it with the real producer's code), then `mismatchShare`, then `requireCoPartitioned`: for every subtopology of the topology, collect the source topics and throw if their partition counts differ.

Read the last test, `same counts but another partitioner...`. It runs your join as three tasks, one per partition, with tiers placed by CRC32. Your check passes, and most orders still find no tier. Which fix from section 4 would make it right?
hints: The versioned table: `builder.table(TIERS, Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()), Materialized.`as`<String, String>(Stores.persistentVersionedKeyValueStore(STORE, HISTORY)).withKeySerde(Serdes.String()).withValueSerde(Serdes.String()))`.

For the global table, Kotlin needs the store type: ``Materialized.`as`<String, String, KeyValueStore<Bytes, ByteArray>>(STORE)``, and the join takes a `KeyValueMapper<String, String, String> { customer, _ -> customer }` before the joiner.

In `requireCoPartitioned`: `topology.describe().subtopologies()`, then `sub.nodes().filterIsInstance<TopologyDescription.Source>().flatMap { it.topicSet() }`. A global table's source isn't in any subtopology, so the global topology passes on its own.

drill.title: An as-of join from memory
drill.prompt: From memory, write a Kafka Streams topology that left-joins `orders` (keyed by customer) with `customer-tiers` so each order gets the tier in force at its own timestamp, keeping 7 days of history. Then answer: c-1 has been silver for 30 days and is gold from 10:00 today, and that upgrade is the table's newest record. What do orders stamped 09:59 today, 10:00 today and 8 days ago get?

recap: Every stream join keeps state from one input and probes it with the other. Stream-stream keeps a window of both sides, stream-table keeps the table, table-table keeps both tables.
A windowed left join can report the record that never found a partner, but only once the window has closed in stream time, so that answer comes late by design.

Joining with the latest table row makes the result depend on arrival order. A versioned table (Kafka Streams 3.5+) or a Flink event-time temporal join uses the version in force at the event's time; a stream-side grace period covers late table updates.
A table-table join is incremental view maintenance: a change on either side is joined with the other side's current state, so one change on a popular row fans out into many updates.

Partitioned joins need both inputs on the same partition count and the same partitioner. Kafka Streams checks the count at start-up but can't see the partitioner; repartition, a foreign-key join or a `GlobalKTable` avoids the problem.
CEP and search on streams store the query and let the data flow past: a pattern becomes a small state machine per key, and a percolator matches each document against stored queries.

quiz.q: A stream-stream left join of authorizations with captures uses a 10-minute window and 1 minute of grace. An authorization for p-9 at 14:00 is never captured. When does `p-9 NOT CAPTURED` come out?
options: At 14:11 on the wall clock
When the first record with a timestamp after 14:11 reaches the join and moves stream time past the window
At once, with a correction later if the capture arrives
Never: left joins only emit matches
quiz.why: The join can only say "no partner" after the window plus grace has passed, and it measures that in stream time, the largest timestamp it has seen. Until a later record arrives, stream time doesn't move. The wall clock plays no part. Kafka Streams 4.x emits non-joined left results only after the grace period, so there is no eager result to correct (the deprecated `JoinWindows.of(...).grace(...)` could emit early spurious ones).

quiz.q: A cashback job joins orders with an unversioned `KTable` of tiers. You rebuild its output from the same two topics and some orders now get a different tier. What happened?
options: The partitions of the two topics interleaved differently, and each order took whichever tier row had arrived before it
The topics were compacted between the runs
The `KTable` was restored from a stale changelog
Kafka Streams joins by processing time, and the clock moved
quiz.why: An unversioned table answers with the latest row by arrival. Across two runs the order in which records from the two topics reach the task can differ, so a late order may see the old tier in one run and the new one in the other. A versioned table makes the answer depend only on timestamps. A stale changelog restore would give wrong state, not run-to-run differences from interleaving.

quiz.q: A `customer-tiers` topic has 3 partitions, produced by a Go service using librdkafka's defaults. `orders` also has 3 partitions, produced by a Java service. A Kafka Streams `KStream`-`KTable` join starts without error. What should you expect?
options: Correct joins: Kafka Streams checked that the counts match
An exception at start-up: the partitioners differ
About two orders in three find no tier, because CRC32 and murmur2 place most keys on different partitions
Correct joins, but slower, because Kafka Streams repartitions automatically
quiz.why: librdkafka's default partitioner hashes keys with CRC32, the Java producer's with murmur2. With 3 partitions, two independent hashes agree about one time in three. Kafka Streams can check partition counts, not partitioners, so it starts and the join silently misses. Set `partitioner=murmur2_random` in the Go service, or repartition one side.

quiz.q: A view joins `cards` (card to account) with `account-tiers` (account to tier) with a foreign-key join. Account acct-5 has 40 cards, and its tier changes. How many records does the view's output topic get?
options: 1: the account's new tier
0: only changes to the left table produce output
41: the old rows deleted, then one merged row
40: one updated row for each card of the account
quiz.why: In a table-table join, a change on either side is joined with the current state of the other. The tier change meets all 40 cards of acct-5, so 40 view rows change. That fan-out is the cost of the second term of the product rule. "Only the left side triggers" is true of stream-table joins, not table-table joins.

quiz.q: From lesson 5: you replace a partitioned `KTable` of merchant tiers with a `GlobalKTable`. Which of these changes?
options: Nothing: both are restored from the same changelog topic
Each instance now holds every merchant, start-up waits for the full table to load, and co-partitioning with the stream no longer matters
The table becomes versioned, so late payments get the right tier
Each instance holds only the merchants of its own tasks, as before, but lookups are faster
quiz.why: A `KTable` is split into tasks, each holding the keys of its input partition. A `GlobalKTable` gives every instance a full copy read from all partitions, bootstrapped completely before processing starts, so any task can look up any merchant and co-partitioning is unnecessary. It has no notion of time, so it doesn't become versioned.

flashcards.front: What state does each kind of stream join keep?
flashcards.back: Stream-stream: a window of both sides. Stream-table: the whole table (latest row per key), nothing of the stream. Table-table: both whole tables.

flashcards.front: In a `KStream`-`KTable` join, which side produces output?
flashcards.back: Only stream records. A table update changes the stored row and emits nothing; orders joined earlier keep what they got.

flashcards.front: What does a versioned table change about a stream-table join?
flashcards.back: The join uses the version with the latest timestamp at or before the stream record's timestamp, instead of the latest row to arrive. Records older than the history retention get null (left join) or are dropped (inner).

flashcards.front: What does `Joined.withGracePeriod` fix that a versioned table alone doesn't?
flashcards.back: Late table updates. It holds each stream record for the grace period in stream time, so a table version that arrives a little late can still be used.

flashcards.front: What does co-partitioning require, and what can Kafka Streams check?
flashcards.back: Same partition count and same partitioner on both inputs. Kafka Streams checks the count at start-up; it can't see the partitioner.
A stored, long-lived pattern query that events flow past, compiled into a small state machine per key, such as three declines then an approval within 2 minutes.

terms.plain: A join of two event streams that pairs records whose timestamps fall within a window of each other.
Enrichment: each event looks up the current row of a table built from a changelog.
A table that keeps each key's past values with their timestamps, so a join can ask for the value as of a time.
Flink SQL's join of a stream with a versioned table as of each row's time (`FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF`).
A table-table join on a field of the left table's value rather than its key.
Two topics with the same partition count and partitioner, so equal keys land in equal partition numbers.
A table that every instance holds in full, read from all partitions of its topic.
Matching patterns across events, such as a sequence within a time limit, with the query stored and the data passing through.

explain_back.prompt: A colleague's cashback job joins orders with a `KTable` of customer tiers. After a replay, finance finds some orders got a different cashback rate than the first time. Explain what went wrong and how you'd fix it, and what the fix costs.
explain_back.answer: An ordinary `KTable` keeps one row per customer, whichever arrived last, and each order looks it up when the order reaches the join. So an order placed before an upgrade but delivered after it gets the new tier. During the replay the two topics' partitions interleaved differently, so some orders saw the other tier: the result depended on arrival order, not on the data. The fix is to join each order with the tier in force at the order's timestamp. In Kafka Streams that means materializing the tiers in a versioned store, which keeps each version with its timestamp for a history retention I'd size from our worst consumer lag. If tier updates can themselves arrive late, I'd add a grace period on the order side so each order waits a little before it's joined. The costs: the store keeps history, so it's bigger, and the changelog can't be compacted down to one row per customer without losing the history; orders older than the retention get no tier; and the grace period delays every order's output by that long.

deeper.body:
**Interval joins and state lifetime in Flink.** A Flink SQL regular join (`a JOIN b ON a.id = b.id`) keeps both inputs in state forever, the first version of section 1. You bound it with a state time-to-live, at the cost of wrong answers for rows older than the TTL. An interval join adds a time condition on both sides (`s.ship_time BETWEEN o.order_time AND o.order_time + INTERVAL '4' HOUR`) and needs append-only inputs; Flink then drops state as the watermark passes, exactly like `JoinWindows`.

**Versioning and compaction pull in opposite directions.** A compacted changelog keeps only the latest value per key, which is all an unversioned table needs. An as-of join needs older versions, so the history has to live somewhere: in the versioned store, for its retention, or in the events themselves. The data-warehouse trick is to give each version an id and put that id in the fact (the order records the tier version it saw), which makes later joins deterministic without any history at join time.

**Spark.** Structured Streaming joins two streams only when you give both sides watermarks and a time condition, so it can drop state; lesson 8 of this track covers its watermarks, and its newer real-time mode doesn't support stream-stream joins at all.

**The book's version.** *Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, 2nd edition, chapter 12, covers the three join types and the time dependence of joins, with slowly changing dimensions as the warehouse answer.
